title: Open Problem (Section 1.1)
statement_text: It is an open problem whether some variation on the local search approach can give PTAS for all monotone FO optimization problems.
context_text: First-order (FO) formulas on graphs use the adjacency relation, finitely many unary predicates (vertex colours), equality, Boolean connectives and quantification over vertices. For a unary predicate $X$, a sentence $\varphi$ is $X$-positive (resp. $X$-negative) if every occurrence of $X$ lies under an even (resp. odd) number of negations, so the solutions are upward (resp. downward) closed. A monotone FO optimization problem is either a positive FO minimization problem (find a minimum set $A$ with $X:=A$ satisfying an $X$-positive $\varphi$; e.g. minimum dominating set, minimum vertex cover, hitting all triangles) or a negative FO maximization problem (maximum set satisfying an $X$-negative $\varphi$; e.g. maximum independent set, maximum $r$-independent set, largest induced subgraph of maximum degree $d$). A PTAS returns, for each fixed $k$, a solution within a factor $1\pm1/k$ of the optimum in polynomial time. Dawar et al. gave PTASes for all monotone FO optimization problems on proper minor-closed classes via Baker's technique and the graph minor structure theorem; the authors prove the same, without the structure theorem, for all classes in which their 'Baker game' (repeated Baker layering interspersed with vertex removal) is won in a bounded number of rounds, which includes all proper minor-closed classes. Cabello and Gajser (proper minor-closed classes) and Har-Peled and Quanrud (classes with polynomial expansion, equivalently strongly sublinear separators) showed that the trivial local search algorithm (repeatedly improving a solution by bounded-size changes) is a PTAS for maximum independent set, minimum dominating set and many related problems. The open problem asks whether a variation of local search gives a PTAS for all monotone FO optimization problems; the paper does not specify the graph classes, presumably those where local search is known to work (proper minor-closed classes or classes with strongly sublinear separators).
